title: Praising Your Team (10 Ways to Do It Better)
author: Ian Frost
summary: Ian Frost, writing around the December reflection point in the school calendar, distills ten principles for delivering praise effectively to school staff, framing it as an underrated leadership skill that rarely appears in formal training or NPQ programmes. He opens with contrasting anecdotes - a headteacher whose patronising praise emptied the room, and another whose carefully balanced words held a Year 11 assembly in rapt silence - to establish that praise is easy to deliver badly and powerful when done well. His ten principles range from mindset shifts (praise is a "renewable resource," not a limited commodity to be rationed) to concrete technique (be specific rather than generic, avoid "blurring the message" with a hidden critique, avoid comparison praise that implicitly diminishes others). He grounds several principles in research, notably the Losada Ratio data showing high-performing teams sustain roughly 5.6 positive comments for every negative one, compared to well under 1:1 in low-performing teams. Frost frames consistent praise-giving as requiring routine rather than spontaneity, recommending leaders build a weekly diary slot for praise nominations so recognition doesn't depend on chance noticing. He closes by tying the whole piece to a broader argument about professional culture: at a moment when inspection frameworks and DfE messaging rarely acknowledge the invisible work of school staff, deliberate praise is a low-cost, high-leverage act of leadership.
points: Frost's central metaphor - a leader as a camera capturing what's already in plain sight but too easily missed - reframes praise as a skill of attention rather than a scarce reward to be rationed out.

He cites the Losada Ratio research showing high-performing teams average 5.6 positive-to-negative comments versus around 0.3-to-1 in low-performing teams, using it as a data case for treating praise as strategically important, not just nice.

His "don't blur the message" principle argues praise should be delivered as a clean, unconditional statement without a hidden "but," since listeners instinctively brace for the qualifier that undercuts genuine positive feedback.
Frost warns against comparison praise ("you were the best speaker today"), noting it implicitly diminishes everyone else being compared and creates future self-consciousness in the person praised.

He closes with an operational fix - a weekly diary slot dedicated to praise nominations - arguing that praise given only when a leader happens to notice something isn't reliable enough to shift team morale.
quotes: A few of years ago I watched a headteacher attempt to praise his staff for something. His patronising tone led to crossed arms and closed faces, and people walked straight out as soon as he finished speaking.
General compliments are next to useless. Instead, describe exactly what your colleague did that you admired, how it made a difference to others.

Most of us know the Losada Ratio (five positive interactions for every negative one), but here’s a less well-known statistic from Losada’s research. The factor that made the greatest difference between the most and least successful teams was the ratio of positive comments to negative comments.
High performing teams averaged 5.6; middle performing teams 1.9; low performing teams 0.3 to 1.

We so rarely hear words of praise which are unadorned with hidden messages. Words always seem to come with additional meanings or subliminal messages. We often wrap a little feedback within a sandwich of vague praise.
Praise, done well, is unconditional. It’s the closest a leader can do to express unconditional affirmation to a colleague.
Offering praise to your team costs nothing, but it does take thoughtfulness and care. And when we get it right, this can motivate your team to perform at their best.
